<reason>B won by neutralizing A's load-bearing premise. A's whole case rested on "once a school writes the check, the employment question is settled," but B drew a clean distinction between payment and legal status (grad fellows, licensing-structured NIL, scholarships staying untaxed), showing the tax/visa/workers'-comp cascade is triggered by the union petition, not the money — and A never re-engaged that distinction after B2, merely reasserting the refuted premise in its closing. B then exposed a real internal contradiction (A1.3 listed transfer rules as CBA subjects; A4.1 claimed playing rules never reach the table), showed wrestlers cannot sit in PRO's bargaining unit on PRO's own payment-based logic, and reframed the antitrust shield as partial under either system. A landed genuine offense — the ratification/consent gap in settlement classes, "partial representation beats none," a credible Big Ten answer to B's direct challenge, and the memorable "bargaining's fruits while refusing the tree" frame — but its later speeches answered B's questions well while letting B's central counter stand. B's two clipped turns are a real execution cost, though the lost substance was largely recovered later.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B2.1–2.2 ("employment is a legal status, not a bank transfer") flipped A's core mechanism and was never substantively re-engaged; compounded by B4.6 catching that A's own opening made transfer eligibility a bargaining subject, undercutting A4.1's "two rulebooks" defense.</best_rebuttal>
